items.title: PM Carney, Xi set to meet amid push for trade concessions and Chinese investment
items.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday morning as the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit gets underway, with trade, energy and investment expected to figure prominently in discussions.

items._ogDesc: Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday morning as the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit gets underway, with trade, energy and investment expected to figure prominently in discussions.
items.body:
SHENZHEN, China — Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday morning as the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit gets underway, with trade, energy and investment expected to figure prominently in discussions.

Driving much of Carney’s international trip is a strategy to diversify Canada’s economy and reduce its reliance on the United States. Part of that strategy has involved what Carney describes as a “warming” of relations with Beijing.

Since Carney’s official visit to Beijing in January 2026, Canada and China have made significant progress on several trade issues.

Canadian merchandise exports to China increased 31.4 per cent in the first half of 2026, reaching $21.5 billion, according to Global Affairs Canada. Canadian crude oil shipments to China have also increased approximately 37 per cent this year.

But several important trade irritants remain, particularly Chinese tariffs on Canadian agricultural products.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

China continues to impose an additional 100 per cent tariff on Canadian canola oil and a 25 per cent tariff on Canadian pork and related products.

There has been significant progress elsewhere. Following Carney’s January visit, China reduced the combined tariff on Canadian canola seed from almost 85 per cent to 14.9 per cent.

Additional tariffs on Canadian canola meal, peas, lobster and crab were suspended. On Nov. 4, the two countries agreed to extend those market-access concessions through the end of 2028.

China has also restored market access for Canadian beef from 20 registered meat establishments.

The question now is whether Carney can secure further concessions from Beijing, particularly on pork and canola oil.

If those tariffs are reduced or removed, China experts will be watching closely to see what Canada offers in return.

Carney has also signalled that he wants Chinese automakers to consider investing in Canadian manufacturing, potentially creating opportunities for Canadian autoworkers who have been affected by U.S. tariffs.

“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Phnom Penh, Cambodia. “If they are not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities.”

Peter Navarro, the White House trade adviser, responded to Carney’s comments on social media.

“Are u really threatening to play China off the U.S.? This is offensive in the extreme. You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive,” Navarro wrote.

Carney has said any Chinese automotive investment in Canada must involve genuine domestic manufacturing, rather than simply assembling vehicles from imported Chinese parts.

“It’s not just about kit cars. There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved,” he said.

The federal government wants Chinese manufacturers to create Canadian jobs and develop domestic supply chains, rather than simply use Canada as an assembly location for vehicles largely manufactured in China.

The January agreement also opened the Canadian market to a limited number of Chinese electric vehicles. Canada replaced its previous 100 per cent surtax with the standard 6.1 per cent most-favoured-nation tariff, subject to an annual quota of 49,000 vehicles.

Beyond trade, the relationship remains complicated by disagreements over foreign interference, cybersecurity, human rights and national security.

Carney has said closer economic engagement with China does not mean Canada is setting aside those concerns.

The two countries established a broader strategic partnership during Carney’s January visit, covering trade, energy, financial services, public safety and other areas of co-operation.

For Carney, the challenge is to expand Canada’s access to the Chinese market while protecting domestic industries and managing an increasingly complicated relationship with its largest trading partner, the United States.

Tuesday’s meeting with Xi will provide another indication of how far that balancing act can go.

items.title: Health Canada urges Canadians to check radon detectors
items.description: Health Canada is warning that inaccurate radon detectors sold online could leave Canadians unaware of dangerous gas levels in their homes.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[This illustration shows radiation hazard symbols beneath houses to represent radon, a naturally occurring, invisible, and odourless radioactive gas that can seep into homes from the ground and is the second-leading cause of lung cancer in Canada after smoking.]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Health Canada is warning that inaccurate radon detectors sold online could leave Canadians unaware of dangerous gas levels in their homes.
items.body:
Health Canada is warning Canadians that inaccurate radon detectors sold online could leave households unknowingly exposed to a radioactive gas linked to lung cancer.

In a public advisory issued Monday, the agency urged homeowners to use approved testing devices, following several warnings and recalls involving electronic monitors that provided misleading readings.

Faulty readings raise health concerns

Radon is a naturally occurring radioactive gas released from the breakdown of uranium in soil and rock. It is invisible, odourless and tasteless, and can accumulate inside homes.

Long-term exposure to elevated radon levels is the second-leading cause of lung cancer in Canada after smoking.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Health Canada said inaccurate detectors can provide readings that are either higher or lower than actual radon concentrations. The biggest concern is that homeowners could receive falsely reassuring results and remain unaware of dangerous exposure.

Previously flagged products include InkBird⁠, Life Basis⁠, Hanchen⁠ and Spolehli⁠ detectors, along with other devices sold on Amazon.ca.

How to test your home

Health Canada recommends testing during winter, when homes are more tightly sealed and radon levels are often higher.

A long-term test lasting at least three months provides the most accurate assessment of a home’s average radon levels.

Consumers should purchase electronic monitors that have passed performance testing by the Canadian National Radon Proficiency Program⁠.

Anyone with a recalled detector should stop using it and dispose of it according to municipal electronic waste requirements.

More information is available in Health Canada’s radon testing guide⁠.

items._ogDesc: Germany’s men’s soccer team was wearing Adidas gear for the last time on Monday as their association of more than 70 years was ending.
items.body:
BERLIN — Germany’s men’s soccer team was wearing Adidas gear for the last time on Monday as their association of more than 70 years was ending.

American sportswear giant Nike is poised to take over next year.

Germany defeated the Netherlands 5-0 in Berlin’s Olympiastadion in their Nations League showdown to be sure of reaching the quarterfinals.

Germany coach Jürgen Klopp wore his usual Adidas cap with the German colours and the slogan “One of 83 million” referencing the country’s population. He’ll likely be forced to find another cap for his next game in charge.

Nike’s takeover caught many by surprise when it was announced in March 2024, with the German soccer federation (DFB) forced to defend the deal running to 2034 from criticism – ultimately it came down to money.

“Nike made by far the best financial offer in the transparent and non-discriminatory tender process,” the DFB said at the time.

It ended an association going back to the 1954 World Cup when Adi Dassler — the founder of the German sportswear brand with echoes of his name — sat on the bench beside West Germany coach Sepp Herberger. The Germans won the trophy for the first time with Dassler’s company’s screw-in stud boots.

Dassler did not invent the boots with changeable studs, as many believe. German shoemaker Alexander Salot came up with that idea and registered his invention with the German patent office on Aug. 30, 1949.

But they did help West Germany beat Hungary in the 1954 World Cup final.

Dassler’s company went on to supply German soccer with its gear ever since. It was worn when West Germany and then the reunified country won another three men’s World Cup titles (1974, 1990, 2014). Germany’s women’s team also wore Adidas gear as it won two World Cup titles in 2003 and 2007.

items.title: Nvidia rules out Jensen Huang comeback as campaign for his return grows
items.description: Nvidia’s board is not weighing a return for Jensen Huang as CEO, sources told Reuters, days after extramarital affairs forced his resignation.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[President Donald Trump, right, presents the National Medal of Science to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during an event at the U.S. Institute of Peace, Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Julia Demaree Nikhinson</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Nvidia’s board is not weighing a return for Jensen Huang as CEO, sources told Reuters, days after extramarital affairs forced his resignation.
items.body:
WASHINGTON — Nvidia’s board is not weighing a return for Jensen Huang as CEO, three people told Reuters, despite a growing campaign for his return days after affairs involving employees and suspected Chinese intelligence ties forced his resignation.

More than 180,200 people have signed a petition demanding Huang’s return, Elon Musk has thrown his support behind the effort, and U.S. President Donald Trump said he would not mind seeing Huang reinstated as CEO. Thousands of people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees have joined the call, even as governance experts and some investors warn that bringing him back before investigations are complete could expose the company to fresh risks.

The groundswell of support for Huang has turned a corporate succession story into a test of whether Nvidia can separate itself from a founder whose influence stretches across its employees — some fiercely loyal to the former CEO — and shareholders, Silicon Valley, the Taiwanese supply chain and Washington.

Taiwan’s tallest skyscraper, Taipei 101, was illuminated on Monday with messages including “Taiwan Loves Jensen.” Some prominent shareholders such as Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker and Altimeter Capital Management CEO Brad Gerstner have urged Nvidia not to rush to replace him before all the facts are known.

“The Nvidia board is not considering bringing Jensen back,” one of the people familiar with the matter said.

The support for the former CEO, who acknowledged having an affair with a Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, comes as U.S. intelligence agencies are still trying to determine the extent of her relationship with China’s Ministry of State Security and what information she may have passed to Beijing, according to two sources familiar with the matter. Evidence gathered so far indicates she was likely an intelligence asset, someone who shared information, rather than a fully trained spy, the sources said.

The uncertainty has divided investors over Huang’s future and complicated the board’s search for a successor. Nvidia shares closed down more than four per cent on Monday, a day before the chipmaker is due to report third-quarter earnings. Since news of Huang’s intimate relationship broke, Nvidia has lost US$800 billion in market value and the stock’s price-to-earnings ratio has dropped to 11.54 from 15.59, well below the 20.8 average for the Nasdaq Composite.

Big names back Huang

The “Stand With Jensen” campaign listed SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney among its signatories. The campaign website showed more than 8,800 signatories identified themselves as current Nvidia employees and more than 94,000 as shareholders, though it cautioned that professional affiliations were self-reported and had not been independently verified.

“We write with gratitude for Jensen Huang and with a clear demand to the Board: bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts,” an open letter on the website said.

Huang stepped down on Thursday after reports of alleged affairs with employees, including one who reported directly to him, plunging the AI chip heavyweight into crisis and sending shockwaves through an industry he helped bankroll.

“I think he learned a big lesson,” Trump said on Monday. Trump’s reported trades this year suggest he held between US$13 million and US$62 million in Nvidia stock as of the end of August, the Washington Post reported on Monday, citing a review of his financial disclosures.

The Trump administration said on Monday it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips, tightening controls as President Donald Trump headed to China for talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Large investors are risk averse

Large investors may prove harder to persuade about reinstating Huang.

One institutional investor in Nvidia stock, speaking on condition of anonymity, said they would be wary of Huang returning to Nvidia, adding that other big companies, including Apple and Microsoft, had thrived after their visionary CEOs had left.

Richard Windsor, an independent technology researcher, said he expected large institutional Nvidia investors to oppose Huang’s return while investigations remained unresolved because of the legal exposure and uncertainty it could create.

“They’re very risk-averse,” Windsor said, but he added that his own view was that Nvidia shareholders would ultimately be better served by Huang’s return because of the relationships he has built with the company’s customers and suppliers.

T Rowe Price analysts said in a note that a transition of power may call for a new organizational structure rather than simply a new executive.

Huang’s exit rocks Taiwan

Huang’s reach is especially visible in Taiwan, where he was born, and where he enjoys celebrity-like status dubbed “Jensanity.”

Nvidia relies on TSMC, which manufactures Nvidia’s most advanced chips, and a sprawling network of suppliers to manufacture the chips and systems underpinning the AI boom.

For many Taiwanese, Huang’s exit marks the loss of a charismatic champion who helped put the island at the heart of the global artificial intelligence boom, with his influence extending well beyond the technology industry.

Jimmy Yang, 42, who works in marketing, said Huang’s departure was a loss for Taiwan, where his influence had extended to local businesses and tourism, and Yang expressed hope that Huang could eventually return to Nvidia.

“His private life is his own choice,” Yang said. “But whether it’s the night market economy he’s driven or his help for the tech industry, it has been massive.”

(Reporting by Ross Kerber, Alexandra Alper, Karen Freifeld and Jeffrey Dastin; Additional reporting by Jaspreet Singh, Wen-Yee Lee, Fabian Hamacher and Erin Banco; Writing by Sayantani Ghosh; Editing by Christian Plumb, Anil D’Silva, Nick Zieminski and Daniel Wallis)

Ross Kerber, Alexandra Alper, Jeffrey Dastin and Karen Freifeld, Reuters

items.title: A technical issue at JPMorgan Chase triggers online banking delays for major U.S. banks
items.description: Thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service Zelle on Monday.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[The Bank of America logo is seen on a branch office, Oct. 14, 2022, in Boston. (AP Photo/Michael Dwyer, File)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Michael Dwyer</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service Zelle on Monday.
items.body:
NEW YORK — NEW YORK — Thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service Zelle on Monday after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.

However, Chase said Monday that the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack, and that it was working to bring banking services back online by the end of the day Monday.

“JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system -- it is not cyber-related,” said Joe Evangelisti, spokesman for the bank.

  • Latest updates on company news here

The disruption comes days after technology troubles affected other parts of the U.S. economy: A major Microsoft outage on Thursday impacted services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot. An outage affecting the nation’s air traffic control system Friday grounded all U.S. flights for several hours and disrupted air travel across the country over the weekend.

On Monday, United Airlines said that it had resolved an internal system outage that delayed departing flights,

In the same statement, Evangelisti said that this was a Chase-only issue.

“This is not a systemic issue -- other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us,” he said.

Monday’s technical issues seemed to be centred at Chase customers and customers at other banks trying to transact with Chase. Those banks, including Bank of America and Citigroup, were not having issues with their banking services.

  • Latest updates on international news here

A spokesman for U.S. Bank said its systems were not directly impacted but that “clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”

Zelle is the peer-to-peer payment system that major U.S. banks use to allow customers to send money to friends and family at near-instant speed. Zelle is owned by Arizona-based Early Warning Services, which in turn is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, U.S. Bank and Wells Fargo.

A spokesman for Early Warning Services said the Zelle network was fully operational.

“An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers,” the spokesman said.

Some Chase customers received a message that said, “Some services aren’t available. We’re working on them. Please try back later.”

Cathy Bussewitz and Ken Sweet, The Associated Press

Correction

This story has been updated to correct Microsoft outage began Thursday, not Friday.

items._ogDesc: Some food and beverage products are being recalled in Canada due to food safety concerns for issues such as the presence of insects and metal pieces.
items.body:
Some food and beverage products are being recalled in Canada due to food safety concerns for issues such as the presence of insects and metal pieces.

The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) recently posted recalls and a food safety warning on its website for the following products.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Producers brand brown rice

Tree of Life Canada is recalling its Producers brand brown rice because of the “presence of insects,” according to the CFIA’s advisory.

“Do not use, sell, serve or distribute the affected product,” the CFIA warned.

The affected products are 22.6 kg packages of brown rice with the Universal Product Codes (UPC) 0 72806 00225 0, and the following codes:

  • 11/09/26, 13326PRM
  • 11/10/26, 13426PRM
  • 12/12/26, 16626PRM
  • 12/14/26, 16826PRM

The product was sold to hotels, restaurants and institutions in Alberta, British Columbia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, Ontario and Quebec.

The CFIA designated it a Class 3 recall. This type of recall means there’s “a low risk that consuming the food may result in any undesirable health problems,” or it “includes food that do not pose a health risk, but that do not comply with legislation.”

Cold Grind organic turmeric powder

The federal agency issued a food safety warning for the Cold Grind brand of organic turmeric powder. It said the product may be unsafe due to the non-permitted colour Sudan I.

“Do not consume, use, sell, serve or distribute affected products,” the CFIA said in a notice online.

The warning is for all 50 g packages with the UPC 6 28110 34220 1.

Those who believe they got sick from consuming the product are advised to contact their health-care provider.

The CFIA said its test results sparked the warning, adding that no illnesses were reported.

“The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) is conducting a food safety investigation, which may lead to the recall of this or other products,” the advisory said.

Archibald’s Nuit Blanche White IPA beer

The Archibald brand Nuit Blanche White IPA is being recalled due to the presence of metal pieces.

“Do not use, sell, serve or distribute the affected products,” according to the CFIA notice.

The following are the affected beer products sold in Quebec:

  • 473 ml pack with UPC 8 76976 00075 3 and all codes starting with J28Q61
  • 4 x 473 ml with UPC 8 76976 00078 4, with codes starting with J28Q61

Quebec-based Archibald Inc. issued the Class 3 recall.

Among other products recently recalled include the popular beers Molson Canadian, Coors Light, Blue Moon due to the presence of metal pieces. The recall covers several alcoholic and non-alcoholic beers made by parent company Molson Canada 2005.

With files from CTV News’ Daniel Otis

items.description: A former United States Ambassador to Canada says he’s optimistic a bilateral deal between the two nations is looming but cautioned Canadians not to expect a Democrat-controlled Congress to reign in President Donald Trump’s tariffs.

MacNaughton, former Ambassador of Canada to the United States, prepares to appear at the Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs and International Development, on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, on Monday, Nov. 16, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Justin Tang]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Justin Tang</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: A former United States Ambassador to Canada says he’s optimistic a bilateral deal between the two nations is looming but cautioned Canadians not to expect a Democrat-controlled Congress to reign in President Donald Trump’s tariffs.
items.body:
OTTAWA — A former United States Ambassador to Canada says he’s optimistic a bilateral deal between the two nations is looming but cautioned Canadians not to expect a Democrat-controlled Congress to reign in President Donald Trump’s tariffs.

David Cohen, who served as ambassador under former president Joe Biden, says Canada and the United States were close to an agreement before trade talks blew up in the eleventh-hour in August.

Appearing by video at the Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs and International Development in Ottawa today, Cohen says Prime Minister Mark Carney was right to walk away.

Cohen says the midterms served as a rebuke of the Trump administration’s policies but it’s unlikely Democrats can achieve the super majority necessary to bypass the president’s veto power over legislation.

Former Canadian ambassador to Washington David MacNaughton, who served during the first Trump presidency, told the committee current negotiations are different and there may be no return to the Canada-U.S. relationship of that time.

He says Canada should look to make a deal with the United States but it must also diversify trade and boost domestic productivity.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

— By Kelly Geraldine Malone in Washington

items.title: 1.5-hour-long system outage forces United Airlines to delay departing flights
items.description: A U.S. system outage that lasted more than 90 minutes forced United Airlines to delay departing flights Monday, just days after a nationwide ground stop.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A United Airlines plane sits at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport in SeaTac, Wash., Monday, Nov. 16, 2026, after a United Airlines system outage. (AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Lindsey Wasson</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: A U.S. system outage that lasted more than 90 minutes forced United Airlines to delay departing flights Monday, just days after a nationwide ground stop.
items.body:
CHICAGO — A system outage that lasted more than 90 minutes forced United Airlines to delay departing flights Monday, just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s network prompted a nationwide ground stop.

Chicago-based United said in a statement that flights that were in the air and flights on its United Express regional network were not affected. The airline also said there was “no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.”

United apologized on social media to customers for the inconvenience. It resolved the issue about one hour and 40 minutes after pilots first began reporting problems to air traffic controllers.

United did not immediately provide details about which of its systems were affected, but pilots told air traffic controllers that the problem was related to a system that helps them determine a plane’s final weight.

Before every departure, pilots use performance software, often on a cockpit tablet, to check that the aircraft can safely take off under current weather and runway conditions. The preflight calculations include the aircraft’s weight along with information about the fuel, baggage, cargo and passengers the plane is carrying.

In August 2025, United grounded planes at major U.S. airports, delaying more than 1,000 flights because of an hourslong outage of a system called Unimatic, which houses flight information that is fed to other systems including those that calculate weight and balance and track flight times.

United said in response to a message from The Associated Press that it had no further information to provide about whether the same system was affected by Monday’s outage.

A recording posted Monday on the ATC app showed a United pilot in Houston asking the tower for permission to stay put at the gate until the system was working again. The app combines live air traffic control radio feeds with real-time visual aircraft tracking.

The flight-tracking website FlightAware showed United with about 600 delayed flights Monday evening, though it was unclear how many were directly related to the system outage.

The United computer problem is just the latest high-profile technology meltdown in recent days.

Earlier Monday, thousands of people reported being unable to access their online accounts at several major U.S. banks after JPMorgan Chase had a technical problem.

On Friday, the FAA ordered every flight grounded because a newly installed router malfunctioned, overwhelming the aging air traffic control system.

And one day earlier, Microsoft experienced a major disruption to its Outlook email service. Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored.

Josh Funk, The Associated Press

items.title: Alberta introduces new electoral boundaries bill, NDP vows court challenge
items.description: Alberta’s United Conservative government is moving ahead with controversial changes to the province’s electoral map, setting the stage for a legal battle over whether the proposed boundaries violate voters’ constitutional rights.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A hot air balloon passes behind the Alberta legislature, in Edmonton, on Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Darryl Dyck]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">DARRYL DYCK</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Alberta’s United Conservative government is moving ahead with controversial changes to the province’s electoral map, setting the stage for a legal battle over whether the proposed boundaries violate voters’ constitutional rights.
items.body:
Alberta’s United Conservative government is moving ahead with controversial changes to the province’s electoral map, setting the stage for a legal battle over whether the proposed boundaries violate voters’ constitutional rights.

Bill 40, the Electoral Divisions Act, would replace Alberta’s existing 87 electoral districts with 91 ridings based on recommendations from an advisory panel whose report was submitted to the legislature Nov. 2.

The legislation follows months of controversy after Premier Danielle Smith’s government rejected recommendations from an independent electoral boundaries commission and appointed a new panel to redraw the map.

If passed, Bill 40 will create several hybrid constituencies combining urban and rural communities, including significant changes in Calgary, Edmonton and Lethbridge.

Justice Minister Mickey Amery says the changes are necessary to ensure Albertans receive effective representation as the province’s population grows.

But Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi says the government is manipulating electoral boundaries for political advantage.

“If this passes, we’re challenging it in court,” Nenshi told reporters Monday.

Nenshi said the party is considering its legal options, which could include seeking an injunction or pursuing an expedited court hearing.

The timing presents an additional challenge, Nenshi said, with Alberta’s next provincial election scheduled for Oct. 18, 2027.

“We are running out of time, and that is an incredibly unfair position to put a judge in, to put the courts in, and to put Albertans in,” he said.

Elections Alberta has previously warned that implementing new boundaries requires extensive preparations, including changes to polling locations, staffing, electoral maps and computer systems.

Constitutional questions

University of Calgary constitutional law professor Kathleen Mahoney says a court challenge could raise fundamental questions about Albertans’ democratic rights, but proving the new electoral boundaries are unconstitutional would require evidence.

Mahoney explained Section 3 of Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms protects a citizen’s right to vote — but there are more protections than simply one’s ability to cast a ballot.

“Section 3’s wording basically says people are entitled to vote, but when that’s been interpreted by the Supreme Court of Canada, they say that effective representation requires more than just ensuring that people can vote,” Mahoney told CTV News.

The Charter also includes consideration of geography, minority rights and the differing interests of urban and rural communities.

“The community interests of people in rural areas are often much different than community interests in urban areas,” Mahoney said, adding that means effective representation aims to ensure those different interests are “reflected in the way in which electoral boundaries are drawn.”

Differences in riding populations don’t automatically violate the Charter, Mahoney said. Rural constituencies may legitimately have fewer voters because of geographical challenges and the difficulty of ensuring residents can be heard.

But she says the government’s decision to replace the original commission’s recommendations creates another issue for the courts to consider.

“If you compare these two reports, you compare the way in which the electoral map has been redrawn, and if it appears that it’s been done not for more effective representation, but for political advantage, then it could run afoul of Section 3 as well.”

Mahoney says lawyers could examine historical voting patterns to determine whether the new boundaries provide an electoral advantage to the sitting UCP government.

If it looks like electoral districts were manipulated for political advantage over effective representation, a judge could find the redrawing of the map to be unconstitutional, she said.

Mahoney says a constitutional challenge could ultimately reach the Supreme Court of Canada, potentially complicating next year’s election. But she says the courts have options to accelerate proceedings in the right circumstances, such as a looming election.

The new boundaries take effect only when the election writ is issued. Mahoney says that wouldn’t necessarily prevent an earlier constitutional challenge.

Ultimately, Mahoney says the issue is about the full meaning of the constitutional right to vote.

“A lot of people just think… filling out a ballot is what they’re given in the Constitution, but they’re given more than that,” she said.

“The right to vote is bigger than that.”

Public interest group prepares to challenge boundaries

Public Interest Alberta is preparing to challenge the proposed electoral boundaries both in the court of public opinion and potentially in the courthouse.

Executive director Bradley Lafortune says the organization is examining a constitutional challenge while also preparing to make its case publicly against the government’s proposed electoral map.

“A Charter challenge is still something that Public Interest Alberta is very seriously considering,” Lafortune told CTV News.

Lafortune says the government’s new maps disregard the extensive public consultation undertaken by the original Electoral Boundaries Commission.

That original commission heard from over 2,000 people, he said. The Nov. 2 report “completely throws (that input) out the window.”

He says the proposed hybrid ridings could leave MLAs struggling to represent constituents with substantially different needs.

Lafortune also questions the significant population differences between some proposed constituencies, arguing they could dilute the voting power of people in more heavily populated urban ridings.

“If I live in rural Alberta, and my riding has 30,000 people in it, but you live in urban Alberta and your riding has 60,000 people in it, my vote counts for a lot more, because I am being represented by an MLA who represents 30,000, you’re being represented by an MLA who represents 60,000,” he said.

Banff-Kananaskis is another proposed constituency that has what he considers problematic boundaries. Highway 40 through Highwood Pass, a key connection between communities in the proposed riding, is closed seasonally.

Lafortune says the organization is considering its options for responding to the legislation, but isn’t prepared to disclose its legal strategy.

He said Public Interest Alberta intends to pursue its concerns independently of political parties.

“This is not a partisan issue, this is an issue of democracy,” he said.

Competing recommendations

The controversy began when the original Electoral Boundaries Commission recommended increasing the number of constituencies from 87 to 89.

Its majority report proposed adding seats in Calgary and Edmonton while eliminating two rural constituencies to reflect population changes.

Commission chair Justice Dallas Miller subsequently recommended increasing the total to 91 seats as a way of preserving the two rural ridings.

The government instead established a new advisory panel, which recommended a substantially different electoral map.

The panel’s November report proposes retaining rural representation while creating additional hybrid ridings that combine portions of cities with surrounding rural areas.

Under the proposal, Lethbridge would be divided among four constituencies instead of its current two, with several of the new ridings extending into surrounding rural communities.

The changes have generated concerns about whether urban and rural voters with different priorities can be effectively represented by the same MLA.

Smith has defended the use of hybrid constituencies, noting they already exist in Alberta, including in her own riding of Brooks-Medicine Hat.

The government says the advisory panel was directed to consider population, geography, transportation, communities of interest and the constitutional requirement for effective representation.

Nenshi maintains the changes are designed to benefit the governing party.

“There’s a very simple rule in a democracy, voters choose their politicians,” he said Monday. “The UCP has tried to have politicians choose their voters.”

The government says the legislation will give MLAs an opportunity to debate the proposed boundaries and provide certainty ahead of next year’s election.

If Bill 40 passes, the new electoral boundaries would take effect when the election writ is issued, expected Sept. 20, 2027, ahead of the scheduled Oct. 18 provincial election.

Whether those boundaries ultimately withstand a constitutional challenge remains an open question.

items._ogDesc: Canada’s inflation rate held steady in October as higher prices for gas, groceries and clothes were partly offset by cheaper cellphone plans and slower rent price growth, Statistics Canada said Monday.
items.body:
OTTAWA -- Canada’s inflation rate held steady in October as higher prices for gas, groceries and clothes were partly offset by cheaper cellphone plans and slower rent price growth, Statistics Canada said Monday.

The annual rate of inflation was steady at 3.1 per cent last month, slightly below economists’ expectations of 3.2 per cent.

The inflation reading raises questions about whether the Bank of Canada will need to raise interest rates again in December, said Benjamin Reitzes, BMO’s managing director of Canadian rates and macro strategist.

“There’s nothing in these numbers at the moment that really screams rate hike for the Bank of Canada,” he said. “They’ve been particularly hawkish over the past few weeks and they raised rates in October and signalled that more could be necessary.”

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

Reitzes said October’s inflation numbers “don’t necessarily signal that they need to do something immediately, but again, that doesn’t mean they won’t. There’s no clearcut case here either way.”

Gasoline continued to be a key driver of headline inflation, rising 30.9 per cent year-over-year in October compared with 27.8 per cent the month before amid continued conflict in the Middle East and Ukraine.

Higher energy costs could eventually push up prices elsewhere, said Royal Bank of Canada economist Abbey Xu.

“The longer energy prices remain elevated, the more cost pressures will filter through to consumer prices with a lag,” she said in a client note.

“The path of energy prices also remains highly uncertain despite the decline in gasoline prices so far in November.”

  • Stay on top of your portfolio with real-time data, historical charts and the latest news on oil

StatCan said gasoline prices rose at a faster annual pace last month partly because prices fell sharply in October 2025, making the year-over-year increase appear larger.

On a monthly basis, however, gasoline prices fell 2.5 per cent in October.

Excluding energy, annual inflation eased to two per cent in October from 2.1 per cent in September.

“Underlying price pressures stayed comparatively contained,” Xu said, noting that the consumer price index excluding both food and energy slowed to 1.8 per cent.

RBC’s diffusion index, which measures how widespread inflation is across the economy, continued to show that “unusually strong price growth has been concentrated in a relatively narrow share of the consumer basket,” she said.

Meanwhile, Canadians once again faced higher prices at grocery stores.

  • How to set BNN Bloomberg as your preferred source on Google

StatCan said the cost of food purchased from stores accelerated to two per cent year-over-year in October after four consecutive months of slower price growth.

Fresh vegetable prices rose 1.4 per cent year-over-year in October after falling 2.9 per cent in September while condiments, spices and vinegars were up 2.6 per cent.

Compared with October 2020, the agency said grocery prices have climbed 31.9 per cent.

Even as inflation slows, Canadians are still feeling the effects of years of rising prices, Reitzes said.

“The reality is inflation is only prices going higher; prices don’t come back down in general,” he said.

“What we need to happen is a lengthy period of relatively low inflation and some good wage growth and that’ll make everyday Canadians feel much better.”

Meanwhile, prices for clothing were up 1.8 per cent in October, driven by a 2.2 per cent year-over-year increase in women’s clothing and a 1.4 per cent increase in men’s clothing.

Clothing prices were up 3.4 per cent month-over-month in October, the largest monthly increase since September 2019.

StatCan said the price increases coincided with higher shipping costs.

In Ontario, prices for natural gas rose three per cent year-over-year in October after declining 18.7 per cent in September.

Prices for cellphone plans fell 6.2 per cent year-over-year in October, after rising 0.8 per cent in September.

StatCan said the decline was largely due to comparisons with a year ago, when companies had raised prices.

Slower rent price growth also helped ease inflation, particularly in British Columbia, while rents in Ontario rose 1.1 per cent year-over-year in October.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

items._ogDesc: Canadian inflation held at 3.1% in October, while property taxes rose 3.8%, outpacing overall price growth as Ontario tax arrears climbed.
items.body:
Canada’s headline inflation remains elevated, but at least it didn’t get worse. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data shows annual headline CPI growth held at 3.1% in October. The lack of acceleration would be good news if not for broadening inflation. Core measures didn’t clarify much this month, but one thing was clear—property taxes are still ripping while arrears climb.

Canadian Inflation Holds At 3.1%, Tamed By Cooling Gas Prices

Annual CPI growth rate.

Annual growth of CPI held at 3.1% in October, remaining elevated but unchanged from September. Helping to tame growth was a deceleration in gasoline prices, which fell 2.5% in the month but were up 30.9% from last year. The agency also notes that annual declines for cellphone plans (-6.2%) helped, though prices may not be lower. Cell phone plans have been a persistent downward pressure due to methodology, not because people are paying less.

Hard Core? Canada’s “Stable” Core CPI Measures Moved Lower, Higher, and Stalled

Canada’s Core CPI measures are designed to provide some clarity, and minimize headline volatility. Unfortunately, Canada’s three big core measures all told a different story last month.

CPI median’s annual growth was unchanged at 2.0%. The core measure tracks the midpoint of price changes, weighted by spending.

CPI-trim slowed from 1.9% to 1.8% in October. This measure excludes the largest upward and downward movements, ideally eliminating the volatility. In practice, prices take the elevator up and the stairs down. As a result, much larger price surges can be neutralized by much smaller declines.

CPI-common accelerated to 2.5% y/y in October, up from 2.4% in September. This measure tracks price movements across categories, filtering out fluctuations for individual items.

No measure is perfect, and the mixed direction reveals how flawed the shift to annual re-indexing has been. The agency’s Census intervals are spaced out to minimize the volatility of resource allocation. However, StatCan argues the pricing of those resources needs to be re-indexed annually.

Canadian Property Tax Growth Slows, But Still Faster Than Inflation

Annual growth of property taxes and special charges.

Every October StatCan’s CPI reports property taxes and other special charges. The segment saw prices rise 3.8% from last year, down from 5.6% reported in 2025. Slower than recent years, but it’s coming down from the sharpest surge since the early ’90s. At the same time, it’s nearly double the BoC’s target rate of inflation, and well above its upper bound of tolerance.

Slower-but-still-elevated property tax and special charges are also unlikely to feel like relief. The 3.3% annual growth in Ontario follows last year’s 5.5% jump. It’s been accompanied by a sharp rise in property tax arrears. Recent filings in the region reveal a property tax arrears rate of up to 11.9% in its largest municipalities.

items.content: <p>Mortgage agent on how she’s helping new buyers break into the market</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0343_639304466007678370.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Mortgage agent on how she’s helping new buyers break into the market
items.body:
First-time buyers who spent years on the sidelines are finally getting into the market as affordability improves and purchase competition eases. We caught up with Mortgage Powered Financial Group mortgage agent Sarita Free at MortgageFest to hear how she’s helping borrowers navigate the current environment.

[00:00] They're finally able to break into the market and stay in their hometown where they've grown up and not have to go elsewhere. It's huge. It helps them qualify for a little bit more. Again, work your book, know your clients. Nothing's just going to be handed to you. So, 2027 is going to be what you make it as a broker.

[00:26] Fergal McAlinden: All right. Well, next up we have our first mortgage agent of the day. We've talked only with lenders so far. So, today we're really happy to have Sarita Free with Mortgage Powered Financial Group.

[00:36] Sarita Free: Yep. It's a mouthful, but you got it.

[00:39] Fergal McAlinden: Good stuff. Is it useful for you as an agent to speak with lenders, get some facetime? I mean, there's a lot of them here today. What type of conversation have you been having?

[00:46] Sarita Free: Well, to be quite honest, I haven't been able to get right in. I'd like to go see some of the tech companies to be fully transparent. Anything that makes my job easier, especially with AI coming out and just stuff to streamline my process.

[01:00] Fergal McAlinden: How about the market so far this year, 2026? We all know it's been an interesting outlook for agents and lenders and everyone. How are you navigating it and what are some of the main things you've been seeing?

[01:11] Sarita Free: Obviously I think my market is special. I'm in Norfolk County, Ontario, and our prices have been pretty stable. A lot of my clients are first-time home buyers and they've finally been able to break in. I am seeing a lot more alternative files on my desk, which is fitting because I'm moderating the alternative panel later. [laughter]

[01:28] Fergal McAlinden: For first-time home buyers, I know for a lot of them this has been kind of the light at the end of the tunnel after what we've been seeing over the past few years. Suddenly, they're in a position to buy. Has that been a big change for you this year?

[01:38] Sarita Free: My book typically has been a lot of first-time home buyers, but yes, this year I'm finding that they're finally able to get into the market. Norfolk County has some great home ownership programs as well. And again, with the 30-year amortization that we can now go to, I find a lot of my buyers that have been on the sidelines, they're finally able to break into the market and stay in their hometown where they've grown up and not have to go elsewhere.

[02:04] Which is huge. Norfolk County, again, it's a special place.

[02:06] Fergal McAlinden: For sure. And that's something that we haven't always seen. People looking to buy have had to go further afield. They haven't been able to stay where they are.

[02:13] Sarita Free: Like a couple of years ago when there were multiple offers and bidding wars. It was so disheartening to have these conversations with people whose family has been in our county for decades and them not being able to break in. So, this year has been really heartwarming and last year, too.

[02:32] Fergal McAlinden: That 30-year amortization is something that I wanted to ask you about. It's really interesting to hear that so many are using that. I know there was a little bit of skepticism about it when it was first unveiled, but every agent and broker that I've spoken to says that's been a really big game changer for buyers.

[02:46] Sarita Free: Yeah, it's huge. It helps them qualify for a little bit more. It makes the payments a little bit more manageable. So it's come in really handy. I'd like to see it in the insurable space. Maybe.

[02:59] Fergal McAlinden: We'll see.

[03:00] Sarita Free: We can hope.

[03:01] Fergal McAlinden: Anything else for first-time buyers? Any other kinds of trends across your desk when you're dealing with them? Are price points okay for them?

[03:09] Sarita Free: Yeah, I think price points are good right now. In more broader markets things have kind of leveled out. Norfolk County as well. I'm really passionate about Norfolk County. It's a smaller market and the majority of my book is there. So, it's a lot different than Toronto and the GTA, but yeah, prices are great and they've absolutely been able to get into the market. It's more affordable now.

[03:31] I don't see bidding wars. And when you do that little trick where realtors price a house really low hoping for that, it does not fly where I'm from.

[03:42] Fergal McAlinden: So, they've got a little bit of time to weigh up their offer and see the property and all that kind of thing.

[03:46] Sarita Free: Exactly. Which is great. Conditions of finance are back in. In-home inspections, everything. You name it. Water testing.

[03:53] Fergal McAlinden: Yeah. We have price reductions, upgrade the electrical, I want a new septic tank.

[03:57] Sarita Free: It's such a good outlook for first-time buyers, which is great.

[04:01] Fergal McAlinden: But it's been a challenging market in some other ways for other buyers and other homeowners as well. We know that renewals are still a big challenge for a lot of people.

[04:10] Sarita Free: Oh, yeah. I see on renewals right now a lot of clients extending their amortization out if it's possible. Going from a jump of an interest rate, goodness, like I had one across my desk the other day, 1.1 to now much higher. Definitely amortizations are being extended in some cases.

[04:28] Fergal McAlinden: That's great. Is there anything this year that you've been keeping top of mind as a broker that maybe wasn't a focus in previous years, or any advice that you would have for agents and brokers navigating the current market?

[04:37] Sarita Free: Right now, work your book. I know you've probably heard that from other agents, but work your book. Stay in contact with your clients. Look for opportunities where their rate might be high. Look for opportunities where they could switch to a new lender for a lower rate. Maybe give them some kind of relief, or refinances, all that kind of stuff. Again, work your book, know your clients.

[05:00] Fergal McAlinden: I'm really interested in hearing from you as an agent. AI, how have you been using that? Has it been a game changer for you? Are you skeptical about it? What way are you approaching it?

[05:09] Sarita Free: No, I'm not skeptical. I think I'm still going to hand in all my files, underwrite all my files, but I'm looking for ways to maybe streamline and speed up repetitive administrative kind of tasks.

[05:22] And actually, I'm interested to see who we have here today that could talk to us about AI. I think there's a panel on AI today, right?

[05:30] Fergal McAlinden: Yes. How about whenever you're looking into your crystal ball, as we say, what do you think is in store for 2027? Are you expecting a busier market or more of the same? What are your thoughts?

[05:41] Sarita Free: I do think it's going to stay steady and get busier, but we're in sales. You get out of it what you put in, right? So, if you want to have a busy 2027, you have to work for it now. Nothing's just going to be handed to you.

[05:55] It doesn't matter. We're in the business of not only purchases and sales, but refinances and switches. There's lots of business out there to be had for every single one of us brokers, every one of us in the room today. So, 2027 is going to be what you make it as a broker.

[06:12] Fergal McAlinden: That's great. Well, thank you very much for joining us today. Really appreciate it, Sarita, and all the best with your panel later on.

[06:18] Sarita Free: Thank you so much.

items.description: Canada’s central bank kicks off its governor search as Macklem rules out a second term
items.content: <p>Canada’s central bank kicks off its governor search as Macklem rules out a second term</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639304443759641224.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Canada’s central bank kicks off its governor search as Macklem rules out a second term
items.body:
Tiff Macklem, the 10th Governor of the Bank of Canada, confirmed Monday he will not seek a second term when his seven-year mandate expires on June 2, 2027.

The Bank’s board has formed a search committee assisted by Zurich-based executive recruiting firm Egon Zehnder, with results expected by spring 2027.

The new governor will be formally appointed by Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne and Prime Minister Mark Carney — himself a former Bank of Canada governor — to take office on June 3, 2027.

“It has been the highlight of my career to serve as the 10th Governor of the Bank of Canada,” Macklem said.

“My time as Governor has seen Canada navigate a more fragmented, shock-prone world. The Bank has faced these challenges by acting decisively, by using sound judgment in the face of uncertainty, and by serving Canadians with humility and a steadfast commitment to its mandate.”

Macklem, 65, took the role on June 3, 2020, with the overnight rate already cut to 0.25% and an emergency bond-purchasing program underway.

His departure was widely expected; no governor had served a second term since 1980.

A legacy shaped by historic rate swings

The defining feature of Macklem’s tenure was Canada’s inflation fight. Consumer prices peaked at 8.1% in mid-2022, prompting one of the Bank’s most aggressive tightening cycles on record — 10 consecutive hikes over 16 months lifted the policy rate from 0.25% to 5%.

After cutting rates, the Bank raised again to 2.5% on October 28, its first hike since 2023.

Jessica Rickerby, president of the Canadian Mortgage Brokers Association of Ontario (CMBA Ontario) in Toronto, said after that move: “While inflation is a key concern of Ontarians, so is housing affordability. The difference is that affordability is a pressing issue right now, whereas inflation is — at present — a hypothetical.”

Who could lead the Bank next — and what it means for brokers

The Bank’s 14-page executive brief for the role sets a high bar for candidates.

Applicants must hold Canadian citizenship and a graduate-level degree in economics, speak both official languages at a high level, and bring experience at the most senior levels of central banking, public policy, financial regulation, or international institutions.

The board has partnered with Quebec economists who joined the Bank of Canada’s inner circle in 2026 and other senior policymakers in shaping the institution Macklem leaves behind.

For brokers navigating Canada’s mounting 2026 mortgage renewal pressures, the transition carries direct weight.

Bruno Valko, vice-president of national sales at RMG Mortgage Corporation in Toronto, recently questioned the Bank’s inflation outlook: “Come 2027, when comparing oil prices to 2026, assuming oil continues to hover around $100 per barrel, I dispute the rationale around how inflation can average 3% when it’s currently 3.1%.”

items.description: New immigration levels won’t overwhelm housing, but Canada’s supply gap stands at 571,000 units
items.content: <p>New immigration levels won’t overwhelm housing, but Canada’s supply gap stands at 571,000 units</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639304410184682267.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: New immigration levels won’t overwhelm housing, but Canada’s supply gap stands at 571,000 units
items.body:
Canada’s residential construction sector is running at a pace sufficient to absorb projected 2027 population growth under the federal government’s new immigration plan, but a supply deficit built during the 2022–2024 surge will take years to clear.

That is the central finding of a new analysis by Rentals.ca, which used Statistics Canada population estimates alongside Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) housing starts and completions data to establish an absorption benchmark.

“At the current pace of about 240,000 starts a year, absorption capacity is approximately 500,000 people,” the report said, based on the ratio that kept supply aligned with population from 1990 to 2015.

Budget 2026 introduced a new immigration levels plan for 2027 to 2029, setting permanent resident admissions at 380,000 annually and adding up to 282,000 one-time and time-limited transitions alongside 370,000 new temporary resident arrivals.

Because most transitions target individuals already residing in Canada, net population growth will be narrower than the headline figures imply.

The report said projected 2027 population growth of 177,000 to 440,000 falls below the 500,000-person absorption capacity of current construction in every scenario modelled.

Kevin Fettig of CMI Financial Group says Budget 2026's housing reforms could improve access to financing for smaller developers, but municipal zoning and approval delays must also be addressed to boost supply. https://t.co/KjzLNLNcY7 — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 11, 2026

The gap left by the 2022–2024 surge

The near-term outlook does not resolve Canada’s deeper structural challenge. The cumulative supply gap — measuring units required above those started to maintain historical construction-to-population ratios — peaked at approximately 780,000 units in mid-2024.

“With population growth slowing and starts holding near 240,000 a year, the gap narrowed to about 571,000 units as of mid-2026,” the report said.

As CMHC’s Fall 2026 Housing Supply Report showed, Canada still requires an estimated 187,000 to 238,000 additional units per year beyond current construction to restore affordability.

Closing the existing deficit under the lowest-growth scenario would take nearly four years of construction above population requirements; under the high-growth scenario, more than a decade.

Construction slowdown may delay rent relief

The report said average national asking rents have declined on an annual basis for 25 consecutive months and are down 5.4% over two years, while the national purpose-built rental vacancy rate climbed to 3.1% in 2025, above its 10-year average.

That cushion is already narrowing: “Asking rents in Toronto and Vancouver are rising for the first time in nearly three years, and the collapse in condo presales will reduce completions in 2028 and 2029,” the report said.

Mathieu Laberge, Chief Economist and Senior Vice President at CMHC in Ottawa, addressed the construction risk directly at the recent Mortgage Professionals Canada National conference in Calgary.

“If we react to a softer market by stopping too much construction, we may be protecting ourselves from today’s risks — but we’re also creating tomorrow’s shortages,” he warned.

“We are at a very high risk that by not providing the appropriate and sufficient supply today, we will lose the improvement in affordability we’ve seen two or three, or five years down the road.”

Laberge also pointed to a structural mismatch in what is being built: “Canada doesn’t simply have too much or too little housing. The reality is that we have a mismatch between the homes people need and the homes the system is producing. What’s small is unaffordable and what’s large is unavailable.”

For brokers advising clients on purchase timing and rental strategy, the report cautioned that newly permanent residents are likely to accelerate household formation, pushing vacancy rates lower before the pipeline fully catches up.

“Pressure on rents and vacancy rates that built up during the surge is therefore likely to ease more gradually than previously projected,” it said.

The bottom line for brokers

The report is broadly constructive in one sense — 2027 isn’t going to see a repeat of the 2022–2024 demand shock. But it is not a signal that the structural supply problem is solved.

The practical read for brokers is that the market remains undersupplied relative to long-run need, rent relief is fragile, and a new cohort of newly permanent residents is about to start forming households and entering the mortgage market.

Getting in front of that client segment now, while also managing the renewal and purchase conversations shaped by a persistent gap, is where the opportunity sits.

items.description: Regulator details kickbacks, a fake inspection and deleted emails behind the penalty
items.content: <p>Regulator details kickbacks, a fake inspection and deleted emails behind the penalty</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0311_638563834459414345.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Regulator details kickbacks, a fake inspection and deleted emails behind the penalty
items.body:
A former Squamish, BC, real estate agent who funnelled buyers to two colleagues in exchange for kickbacks must pay $627,000.

The BC Financial Services Authority (BCFSA) also cancelled his licence in a sanctions decision dated Oct. 28 and made public Nov. 13.

The order against Andre Zubko and his personal real estate corporation stems from a commission scheme he ran across eight home sales in 2016 and 2017. It combines $320,000 in discipline penalties with $307,000 in enforcement expenses.

Zubko’s licence renewal was denied in 2017, and he has not been licensed since.

How did the commission scheme work?

Zubko was licensed from 2006 to 2017 and worked at One Percent Realty, a flat-fee brokerage.

According to the decision, he sent unrepresented buyers to a high school acquaintance and to a cousin of a family member. Those agents wrote offers demanding a higher buyer’s commission, then passed most of it back to him.

Sellers paid more than $50,000 in extra commissions, and Zubko collected $47,641.23 in kickbacks.

Two deals went further. In one, Zubko persuaded a seller to cut the price of a lot sold to his family member from $350,000 to $175,000. The contract was assigned days later for $335,000, a $160,000 gain.

In another, he invented a home inspection to push a price down from $807,000 to $797,000, even though he knew the contract had already been assigned for $845,000.

“It is difficult to imagine a more clear-cut case of deception of one’s client than completely making up a negative home inspection in order to convince that client to sell their property at a lower price,” Senior Hearing Officer Andrew Pendray wrote.

During the investigation, Zubko deleted emails, met with others involved to align their accounts, and gave investigators false statements.

Canadian Mortgage Professional reported the regulator’s original misconduct findings in 2024. 

FSRA's has permanently removed a former mortgage agent's licence and imposed administrative penalties after findings related to unlicensed mortgage activity, improper compensation arrangements, and facilitating dishonesty. https://t.co/Wjos9A5fUi — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 3, 2026

What the penalty signals for BC brokers

Four transactions fell under the rules in force before Sept. 30, 2016, which capped penalties at $10,000.

For the remaining four, Pendray assessed $550,000, then cut it by 50% to $275,000. He cited proportionality and Zubko’s years without a licence.

He added $35,000 to strip out any remaining profit and set enforcement costs at 65% of the regulator’s expenses.

Zubko had proposed about $85,000 in penalties and $40,000 in costs.

Limiting fines to client losses, Pendray wrote, would turn them into “just the cost of doing business in an inappropriate way, and only if one was caught.”

The ruling lands weeks after BC’s Mortgage Services Act took effect on Oct. 13, completing the province’s overhaul of mortgage broker regulation.

The regulator has also acted against individual brokers, including one barred for falsifying clients’ income records. 

Zubko has 30 days from the decision to appeal to the Financial Services Tribunal and 60 days to pay.

items.title: October inflation steady, complicating BoC’s December call
items.description: Canada’s October CPI held flat, raising doubts over another Bank of Canada rate hike
items.content: <p>Canada’s October CPI held flat, raising doubts over another Bank of Canada rate hike</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639304381242559284.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Canada’s October CPI held flat, raising doubts over another Bank of Canada rate hike
items.body:
Canada’s annual inflation rate held at 3.1% in October, matching September’s reading and coming in just below the 3.2% most economists had expected. The data has now tilted the debate toward a potential pause at the Bank of Canada’s (BoC) December 9 rate decision.

Statistics Canada reported Monday that the consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.2% on a seasonally adjusted basis month over month in October.

Upward pressure from gasoline, groceries, clothing, and natural gas was partially offset by cheaper cell phone plans and slower rent growth.

Excluding energy, the CPI rose 2.0% year over year, edging down from 2.1% in September.

Gasoline remained the dominant inflationary driver, rising 30.9% year over year from 27.8% in September, reflecting a base-year effect tied to lower crude oil prices in October 2025.

Despite that headline figure, pump prices fell 2.5% month over month. Grocery price growth ticked up to 2.0% year over year from 1.7%, breaking a four-month easing streak, with fresh vegetable prices rising 1.4% after declining 2.9% in September.

Clothing costs climbed 1.8% year over year, the largest monthly increase since September 2019, with Statistics Canada attributing the move to higher shipping costs.

Excluding food and energy, the CPI eased to 1.8% year over year.

Canada’s labour market shed 4,700 jobs in October, pushing the national unemployment rate to 6.7% from 6.5%, a third consecutive month of deterioration that is now complicating the Bank of Canada’s (BoC) path to a December rate hike. https://t.co/M8Ce4IYrjH — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 10, 2026

Economists split on December

The BoC’s preferred core measures — CPI-trim at 1.8% and CPI-median at 2.0% year over year — held at or below the 2% target. The case for holding at December 9 has strengthened, though the question is not fully settled.

Andrew Grantham, senior economist at CIBC Economics in Toronto, was direct: “Today’s tame inflation report, combined with the recent move lower in gasoline prices and signs of weakness in the labour market, suggest that there’s no need for the Bank of Canada to rush another interest rate hike and supports our call for a hold in December.”

RBC Economics’ Abbey Xu, based in Toronto, retained a more cautious outlook. Her base case remains a 25-basis-point hike to 2.75% at the December meeting, “although further downside surprises in growth, employment or inflation could still give policymakers reason to pause.”

Leslie Preston, senior economist at TD Economics in Toronto, characterised the BoC’s October 28 move to 2.5% as pre-emptive: “The Bank of Canada raised interest rates in October to get ahead of an expected uptick in inflation in Canada, but the signs of hotter price gains were fairly lukewarm in October.”

What it means for brokers

Bond yields and the Canadian dollar both fell Monday following the release, signalling that markets are trimming expectations of a December hike.

For mortgage professionals across Canada, the December 9 announcement will carry unusual weight for client conversations and product strategy.

Three consecutive monthly job losses, softer-than-expected third-quarter GDP growth, and declining gasoline prices, as flagged by RBC’s Xu, now all argue for patience from the BoC.

Whether core inflation broadens enough over the next three weeks to justify another rate increase will determine whether Canada’s mortgage market greets 2027 at 2.5% or 2.75%.

items.body:
Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Canadian Immigration Changes To Double Population Growth Rate: BMO

Canada’s looking to boost its immigration, but it hasn’t framed it that way. Officially, the target is to add 380,000 new permanent residents per year for 2027-29. However, BMO economists estimate that special measures push the total to 660,000 for 2027. The massive change has the bank nearly doubling its population growth forecast. Though it’s worth distinguishing between a target and reality. Canada’s foreign student tapering only began after applications dropped sharply, suggesting exhausted demand.

Canadian Housing Affordability’s Record Recovery May End Soon: NBF

Housing affordability across Canada has made a record 11 straight quarters of improvement. That sounds impressive, but the details are less flattering. Mortgage payments on a typical home would consume 50.9% of a median household’s income at this level. Even with the record length of improvements, this is still one of the worst markets for buyers in history. National Bank economists warn this may also be as good as it gets in the near-term, as mortgage rates are set to climb.

Canada To Add 200,000 Permanent Resident Spots, Housing Boost Limited

Canada’s immigration plan will boost permanent residents 50% higher than the headline data suggests. It’s seen as a boost to the economy, especially housing demand, but that may not be the case. The added capacity targets those already in the country and looking to stay. While this can mean less churn and ultimately more people, demand doesn’t get a direct boost. Their consumption is already reflected in the current data.

Ontario Real Estate

Ontario Property Tax Arrears Hit 24-Year High, Brampton Leads At 11.9%

Ontario property tax arrears are at a 24-year high, driven by Toronto’s suburbs. Filings show the property tax arrears rate hit 7.2% of the $34.1 billion in levies for 2025, up 2.46 points since 2019. The rate is now at its highest level since 2001, but there’s an important distinction here. Today, the rate is climbing, but back then it was falling after the early ‘90s real estate bubble popped. Coincidentally, property taxes just made their biggest increase since the early ’90s.

Toronto Real Estate

Over 1 In 8 Greater Toronto Rental Units Sit Vacant As Completions Hit A Record

Greater Toronto’s rental construction boom means a lot of supply is sitting empty. The often-reported vacancy rate for stabilized purpose-built rentals fell from 5.4% to 3.0% in Q3. The catch is stabilized, which excludes buildings that have never hit 95% occupancy. In a normal market, it may not be a big difference; including all purpose-built units means a 13.3% vacancy rate. Even with 1 in 8 units vacant, there are 34,545 more currently under construction, nearly half of the units being built across Canada. So far, there’s been minimal progress on prices, but that can change fast with a record supply glut on the way.

items.body:
The Ontario real estate correction has another ominous point—unpaid property taxes. Filings with the Government of Ontario show municipalities are still struggling to collect $2.43 billion in overdue property taxes at the end of 2025. The filings show the arrears rate of property taxes is now at the highest level since 2001.

About Today’s Data

Today, we’re looking at the 2025 property tax arrears rate for Ontario municipalities. This is the share of each year’s levy that was still unpaid at year’s end, according to each municipality’s filings. For the provincial rate, we’re using the 316 out of 414 municipalities that filed in 2025, and 392 that are up to date for 2024. While this covers the lion’s share of dollar value, Hamilton’s filings are notably unavailable. The city’s 2024 filing was also unavailable, so it appears someone is behind on their homework.

Ontario Property Tax Arrears Hit Highest Level Since 2001

Ontario property taxes in arrears: Delinquent property taxes as a share of total property tax levies, 2000 to 2025.

Source: Government of Ontario; Better Dwelling.

Ontario’s arrears rate hit 7.2% of 2025 property taxes, representing $2.4 billion of the $34.1 billion in levies. The rate is a sharp jump of 48 basis points (bps) from 2024 and 246 bps since 2019. It’s the highest arrears rate for the province since 2001, making it a generational high. A key difference here is that the rate was falling back then, whereas today it’s rising—and where it stops is anyone’s guess.

Ontario’s Major Cities See Property Tax Arrears Hit Up To 11.9%

Property taxes in arrears: Delinquent property taxes as a share of total property tax levies, 2025. Largest municipalities with up-to-date filings.

Source: Ontario municipality filings; Better Dwelling.

Out of Ontario’s largest cities with filings, Brampton’s 11.9% arrears rate is by far the highest in the province. It’s followed by Vaughan at 9.9%, and Kitchener at 8.9%. All three cities have been above average in recent years, and they’re unusually high.

Brampton’s rate is its highest since 2004, while Vaughan and Kitchener are at their highest since 2001. Brampton also went from below average in 2021 to the highest of the large cities in just four years.

In contrast, Toronto’s 2025 property tax arrears rate of 6.6% is somewhat outperforming. The City represents over 1 in 5 dollars of 2025 property taxes in arrears, but levies nearly a quarter of the province’s property tax. In the provincial context, it’s better than average. However, benchmarked against itself, this is the city’s highest rate since 2001. Once again, the difference here is that the rate was falling back then after property taxes in arrears quadrupled from 1988 to 1993 over the six cities that are now Toronto.

It’s probably not a coincidence that property taxes and special levies just made their largest jump since the early ’90s, either. Everyone loves a fast-growing city when the market is booming, but not so much once it’s time to pay those bills.

items.title: How the Microsoft chaos impacted Canada’s mortgage industry
items.description: Brokers report varying levels of disruption as Microsoft 365 outage spread
items.content: <p>Brokers report varying levels of disruption as Microsoft 365 outage spread</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639301912201989264.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Brokers report varying levels of disruption as Microsoft 365 outage spread
items.body:
Microsoft appears to finally be getting to grips with the issues that caused huge global outages in its Microsoft 365 services on Thursday and Friday, but that chaos led to its fair share of disruption across the world – and the mortgage industry.

Brokers were forced to find workarounds as email disruptions delayed closings and left lenders and lawyers unable to receive documents, raising questions about whether various industries were fully prepared for such a crisis.

David Clarke, a Nova Scotia-based mortgage broker, told Canadian Mortgage Professional his exposure was limited because he operates a personal Gmail account alongside a Microsoft-based email system, but the outage still required him to pick up the phone and clarify things with industry counterparts.

“I had a lender where I was sending stuff and they weren’t getting it,” he said. “But I was aware of the outage, so I called and we navigated it. It’s kind of weird – it was like some things got through and some things didn’t.”

Clarke said he first noticed something was up yesterday when a lawyer requested identification documents for a refinance, but never received them. In that case the delay had no consequences, but he noted how quickly the outcome could change for a purchase closing with a hard deadline.

Another problem: many professionals might not have realized they were missing anything at all. “It’s a pretty big deal,” Clarke said. “Even people that knew about the outage, they wouldn’t know that someone was trying to send them something. So it’s hard to even react to it.”

Brokers find workarounds as challenges persist

Other brokers using Gmail also saw minimal disruption, although they had to manoeuvre challenges with clients or industry partners whose platforms were affected.

Paul Meredith, principal broker and president at PMT Mortgage Corp. in Toronto, told CMP he noticed a marked drop in incoming emails even though his team is on Gmail. “We’ve been following up with clients and anything of importance by phone and text,” he said. “We’ll always do everything we can to work around life’s unexpected challenges.”

His primary concern is with enquiries that arrive during the blackout period. “I think the biggest issue here would be if there are any new inquiries trying to email us,” he said. “But they would certainly be aware of the outage so would generally call, text, or wait it out.”

For some brokers, the outage had zero effect on day-to-day operations. “Honestly, this did not impact us at all,” Taz Zaide of 6ix Mortgage Group said. “Everything moved along as usual just like any other day on our end.”

Outage compounds mortgage industry’s staffing problems

One factor that extends well beyond any single outage, Clarke said, is an industry already running short on staff. “Every [part of the] industry is so understaffed,” he said. “Everyone’s busy. So for you to even notice that you didn’t get something, you’ve got to be pretty proactive on a file to check in.”

Most professionals are reacting to emails, he said, rather than monitoring for their absence. “If I was on the road yesterday, I would have probably missed things,” he said.

The disruption extended across the mortgage industry globally. The impact was immediate and widespread for Katherine Stagg, founder and managing director of Stagg Mortgage Services in the United Kingdom.

“I didn’t actually realize how much I relied on it until it doesn’t work,” she told Mortgage Introducer. “Everything is based on your calendar, your emails, your Copilot – everything you can’t do.”

At the time of writing, Microsoft appearsto be making progress in restoring access to its platforms, although that “broad recovery” is still not complete.

Clarke said the lesson for the mortgage industry is a deeper one than technical fixes. “Things like this happen and you’ve got to be nice to people while they happen,” he said.
